title: Three kinds of understanding, resolve and happiness

verses.sa: प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च कार्याकार्ये भयाभये । बन्धं मोक्षं च या वेत्ति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥
verses.tr: O Partha, the intellect that knows what leads forward and what withdraws, what should be done and not done, what is fear and fearlessness, what binds and what frees, is sattvic.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is sorting the mind into types. Listen for the one word that names the tool of knowing.

body.text: O Partha, the intellect that knows what leads forward and what withdraws, what should be done and not done, what is fear and fearlessness, what binds and what frees, is sattvic. The word buddhi, intellect, appears in the verse, and the verse says it knows. It is a knowing that separates action from withdrawal, duty from non-duty, fear from fearlessness, and bondage from freedom. Krishna now turns to the mind that mistakes action for right action and non-action for wrong action, calling it rajasic.

verses.sa: यया धर्ममधर्मं च कार्यं चाकार्यमेव च । अयथावत्प्रजानाति बुद्धिः सा पार्थ राजसी ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna, the intellect that does not truly know right action and wrong action, duty and what should not be done, is rajasic.
verses.angle: Rajasic buddhi cannot tell duty from non-duty
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just described the sattvic intellect that sees clearly what frees and what binds. Now he turns to the mind that lacks that clarity.

body.text: Arjuna, the intellect that does not truly know right action and wrong action, duty and what should not be done, is rajasic. Krishna warns that a rajasic intellect gets dharma and adharma wrong. It cannot tell the difference between duty and what to avoid, and so it misreads the right action. Krishna next describes the intellect that is completely covered by darkness and calls wrong action right.

verses.sa: अधर्मं धर्ममिति या मन्यते तमसाऽऽवृता । सर्वार्थान्विपरीतांश्च बुद्धिः सा पार्थ तामसी ॥
verses.tr: The mind covered by darkness calls wrongdoing right and reverses everything.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna moves from the confused to the darkest understanding. Listen to how a mind completely covered by darkness names evil as good.

body.text: The mind covered by darkness calls wrongdoing right and reverses everything. The word tamasi, covered by darkness, is the engine of this verse. It is the darkness itself that makes the buddhi call adharma righteous and reverse every aim. Krishna now turns to the steadiness that holds the mind, senses, and life-force in place through yoga.

verses.sa: धृत्या यया धारयते मनःप्राणेन्द्रियक्रियाः । योगेनाव्यभिचारिण्या धृतिः सा पार्थ सात्त्विकी ॥
verses.tr: O Partha, that steadfastness by which one holds steady the functions of mind, life-force, and senses through unwavering yoga is sattvic steadfastness.
verses.angle: Sattvic dhriti steadies mind and senses
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is now answering the question, what is true inner strength? Listen to how he names the one strength that keeps the mind, breath, and senses steady.

body.text: O Partha, that steadfastness by which one holds steady the functions of mind, life-force, and senses through unwavering yoga is sattvic steadfastness. Sattvic dhriti holds mind, breath and senses steady through unwavering yoga, Krishna tells Arjuna. Krishna now turns to the steadiness that clings to pleasure and wealth while craving results, which he calls passionate.

verses.sa: यया तु धर्मकामार्थान् धृत्या धारयतेऽर्जुन । प्रसङ्गेन फलाकाङ्क्षी धृतिः सा पार्थ राजसी ॥
verses.tr: Arjuna, the steadiness that clings intensely to duty, pleasure, and wealth, while craving results, is passionate steadiness.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is sorting out the different kinds of inner steadiness a person can have. Listen to how he describes the passionate kind.

body.text: Arjuna, the steadiness that clings intensely to duty, pleasure, and wealth, while craving results, is passionate steadiness. Krishna names a lower steadiness that still holds dharma but for reward. It is still discipline, but mixed with craving. Krishna then turns to the lowest kind of steadiness, where a dull mind clings to sleep, fear, and pride.

verses.sa: यया स्वप्नं भयं शोकं विषादं मदमेव च । न विमुञ्चति दुर्मेधा धृतिः सा पार्थ तामसी ॥
verses.tr: The dull-minded one does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, sorrow, and pride. That steadfastness is tamasic, Arjuna.
verses.angle: dhriti: the stubborn resolve of a dull mind
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna is listing the qualities of resolve, and he names the lowest kind. Listen for the word that means the stubborn grip of a dull mind.

body.text: The dull-minded one does not let go of sleep, fear, grief, sorrow, and pride. That steadfastness is tamasic, Arjuna. The word to hear is dhriti, steadfastness. Here it is tamasic, a dull resolve that will not let go of sleep, fear, grief, and pride. Krishna now turns to the three kinds of happiness, starting with the one that first feels like poison.

verses.sa: सुखं त्विदानीं त्रिविधं श्रृणु मे भरतर्षभ । अभ्यासाद्रमते यत्र दुःखान्तं च निगच्छति ॥
verses.tr: O best of the Bharatas, hear from me now about three kinds of happiness. The happiness that comes from practice, ends sorrow, and first feels like poison but later like nectar is called sattvic.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna finishes his teaching by pointing to a happiness that grows through practice. Listen to how he describes its end.

body.text: O best of the Bharatas, hear from me now about three kinds of happiness. The happiness that comes from practice, ends sorrow, and first feels like poison but later like nectar is called sattvic. Krishna begins on the three kinds of happiness: sattvic joy grows with practice and brings an end to sorrow. Krishna then turns to the happiness that seems like poison at first and like nectar in the end.

verses.sa: यत्तदग्रे विषमिव परिणामेऽमृतोपमम् । तत्सुखं सात्त्विकं प्रोक्तमात्मबुद्धिप्रसादजम् ॥
verses.tr: That happiness is called sattvic, which seems like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from clarity of the discerning mind and the peace of inner understanding.
verses.angle: Amrit: the nectar of sattvic happiness
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna continues by describing the first of the three kinds of happiness, using a single striking image.

body.text: That happiness is called sattvic, which seems like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from clarity of the discerning mind and the peace of inner understanding. Krishna pairs two words, visha, poison, and amrita, nectar. The highest happiness begins as poison and ends as nectar, showing that true joy can feel bitter at first. Krishna now turns to the second kind of pleasure, the one that begins like nectar but ends like poison.

verses.sa: विषयेन्द्रियसंयोगाद्यत्तदग्रेऽमृतोपमम् । परिणामे विषमिव तत्सुखं राजसं स्मृतम् ॥
verses.tr: The pleasure that begins like nectar from contact between the senses and their objects, but ends like poison, is called rajasic pleasure.
verses.angle: Nectar at first, poison at the end
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just described a steady, lasting joy. Now he names the pleasure that tempts us, born from our senses touching the world. Listen for its two stages.

body.text: The pleasure that begins like nectar from contact between the senses and their objects, but ends like poison, is called rajasic pleasure. Krishna gives two exact words, agraha, at first, and pariname, in the end. The pleasure starts like nectar, but it ends like poison, and that is why it is called rajasic. Krishna now turns to the third kind of pleasure, one born of sleep, laziness, and negligence.

verses.sa: यदग्रे चानुबन्धे च सुखं मोहनमात्मनः । निद्रालस्यप्रमादोत्थं तत्तामसमुदाहृतम् ॥
verses.tr: That pleasure, born of sleep, laziness, and negligence, deludes the self at the beginning and at the end; it is called tamasic.
verses.angle: Tamasic pleasure deludes the self from start to finish
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna finishes sorting the three kinds of pleasure. Listen to how he describes the lowest one.

body.text: That pleasure, born of sleep, laziness, and negligence, deludes the self at the beginning and at the end; it is called tamasic. Krishna points to a pleasure born of sleep, laziness, and negligence, and says it deludes the self from the very beginning to the very end. Krishna then reminds us that no being on earth is free from these three qualities.

verses.sa: न तदस्ति पृथिव्यां वा दिवि देवेषु वा पुनः । सत्त्वं प्रकृतिजैर्मुक्तं यदेभिः स्यात्ित्रभिर्गुणैः ॥
verses.tr: There is nothing on earth, in heaven, or among the radiant beings that is free from the three qualities born of nature.
verses.angle: Guna: no realm is exempt from nature's three strands
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Listen for one word that covers every realm of existence. Krishna is about to explain that no being is exempt from the three gunas.

body.text: There is nothing on earth, in heaven, or among the radiant beings that is free from the three qualities born of nature. Notice the word gunaih, three qualities. Krishna lists earth, heaven, and the gods to show the scope is total; no being in the material order is exempt. Krishna then explains how the four social duties are divided according to these same three qualities.

verses.sa: ब्राह्मणक्षत्रियविशां शूद्राणां च परंतप । कर्माणि प्रविभक्तानि स्वभावप्रभवैर्गुणैः ॥
verses.tr: O scorcher of foes, the duties of priests, warriors, merchants, and workers are divided according to the qualities born of their nature.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just told Arjuna that every being is woven from three qualities. Now he names the four kinds of people who act from those qualities. Listen to how he calls them.

body.text: O scorcher of foes, the duties of priests, warriors, merchants, and workers are divided according to the qualities born of their nature. Krishna speaks to Arjuna, the warrior, and calls him parantapa, scorcher of foes. In this same breath, he lists the four classes of people, showing that the structure of society is as natural as the qualities that drive it. Krishna continues by showing that the natural duty of a brahmin is self-control and knowledge.

verses.sa: शमो दमस्तपः शौचं क्षान्तिरार्जवमेव च । ज्ञानं विज्ञानमास्तिक्यं ब्रह्मकर्म स्वभावजम् ॥
verses.tr: Self-restraint, control of the senses, austerity, purity, forgiveness, honesty, knowledge, realization, and faith in the supreme reality are the natural duties of a brahmin.
verses.angle: Brahmins begin with shama and dama
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: Krishna has just shown how every human nature carries its own work. Now he turns to the inner qualities that define a Brahmin's path.

body.text: Self-restraint, control of the senses, austerity, purity, forgiveness, honesty, knowledge, realization, and faith in the supreme reality are the natural duties of a brahmin. The words shama, control of the mind, and dama, control of the senses, appear together here, and they reveal that a Brahmin's work is rooted in mastering the inner self. Krishna now turns from the qualities of a brahmin to the outer life of a warrior, listing the qualities that define a kshatriya.

verses.sa: शौर्यं तेजो धृतिर्दाक्ष्यं युद्धे चाप्यपलायनम् । दानमीश्वरभावश्च क्षात्रं कर्म स्वभावजम् ॥
verses.tr: Valor, radiance, firmness, quick skill, never fleeing in battle, generosity, and leadership are the natural duties of a warrior.
verses.speaker: Krishna

intro.text: If a thinker's work is self-control and knowledge, what is a warrior's work? Listen to the list of qualities that belong to a kshatriya.

body.text: Valor, radiance, firmness, quick skill, never fleeing in battle, generosity, and leadership are the natural duties of a warrior. Valour, vigour, firmness, skill, not fleeing battle, generosity and leadership make up the kshatriya's natural duty. Krishna then lists the natural work of farmers, cattle-herders, and merchants.

prev.title: Knowledge, action and the doer, in three kinds
